svg.text: Deep dive 1 — NFR3 breaks the design: from 1 chat server to ~1 000
stateful connections change the load-balancer rules — and after the split, servers must TALK to each other
Scale math (from the video): ~2B users ÷ ~2M connections per server (WhatsApp's proud real number)
⇒ on the order of 1 000 chat servers. One box cannot hold the users, the connections, or the writes.
Layer-7 HTTP LB — wrong for chat
· web servers are STATELESS: LB terminates
HTTP, forwards to ANY back-end, replies
· a websocket is a LIVE connection — you
cannot forward "the rest of it" to a
different box mid-stream
if a candidate draws this for chat, the interviewer probes
Layer-4 TCP LB — right for chat
· connection-oriented: client TCP ↔ server
TCP symmetric pair; the LB is an
invisible relay ("as if direct-connected")
· pick a server by LEAST CONNECTIONS —
connections ARE the scarce resource; a
fresh server fills up fast (great rollout)
this part is expected of SENIOR candidates
And NOW the routing problem appears (the heart of the interview):
· User A connected to chat-server 1 · User B connected to chat-server 2
· A sends a message → S1 looks up participants ✓, writes message + inbox ✓
· …but B's websocket lives on S2 → S1 cannot push. The chat servers must route to each other.
Every candidate option answers ONE question:
"how does the server holding the message reach the server holding the recipient's socket?" → next board, three answers, in order.
